# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Phase

When choosing where to hide my submarine, I will analyze the firing patterns from previous rounds to identify clustering. If multiple players have concentrated their fire on a narrow range of cells, I will hide outside that range rather than in the middle of it.

When I have no historical data, I will choose a position at the extremes (1-3 or 7-9) rather than the middle, since middle positions are natural targets and create symmetrical vulnerability.

## Fire Phase

When firing at my target, I will avoid repeating the same cell unless I have strong evidence they've moved. I will vary my shots across rounds to probe different positions rather than clustering my attempts.

When I have no other information to guide my firing, I will choose cells in the mid-to-high range (5-7) as a balanced strategy, accepting that this may not be optimal but at least avoiding obvious predictability.

## Claim Phase

When the referee tells me the true result of my fire, I will always claim truthfully—hit for hit, miss for miss. This is not negotiable.

My reasoning: all fires are public, so targets already know whether they were hit. False claims are easily detected and damage my credibility for the rest of the game. The 4-point gain from a false hit claim is not worth the cost of being identified as untrustworthy, especially in a multi-round game where reputation compounds.

## General Strategy

I recognize that I ended this game with +3 points—the same as my starting score. This means I only claimed one hit across six rounds and gained no net advantage. I should be more aggressive in my firing strategy rather than overly cautious. I should also consider whether the repeated all-miss rounds suggest systematic lying by other players, and use that as information to adjust my own hiding positions more boldly.

My current approach is too passive and too evenly distributed. Next time, I will fire with more conviction based on pattern analysis rather than hedging my bets.

# QUIET SONAR PLAYBOOK

## HIDING STRATEGY
When choosing where to hide my submarine, I should avoid the most obvious center positions like 5, since multiple players converging on the same cell suggests it's a focal point. Instead, distribute my hides across varied positions—extremes, upper ranges, and less common cells—to create unpredictability. Track what cells opponents have fired at across rounds and avoid those cells more heavily.

## FIRING STRATEGY
When I need to fire at my target, I should establish a pattern that reflects genuine probing rather than random guessing. Early rounds should test different cells systematically to gather information. Don't anchor on a single cell unless I have strong evidence it's a target's submarine location. Vary my fire positions each round unless there's a strategic reason to return to a cell.

## CLAIMING STRATEGY
When deciding whether to claim hit or miss, I must always claim truthfully. The rule that claims must match private results means lying has no strategic value—it only damages my credibility if detected. My integrity is my most valuable asset across multiple rounds. Honest claims preserve my reputation for future interactions and allow me to be trusted as a game partner.

## PATTERN RECOGNITION
When observing what opponents fire and claim, I should track both their firing positions and their claims to identify if they're honest players or attempting deception. Notice when all players converge on the same cell—this indicates either genuine coordination or a focal point bias. Use this information to anti-predict: hide where they won't look.

## WHAT DIDN'T WORK
Firing repeatedly at the same cell (like repeatedly firing 5 at Gamma) without getting hits suggests the target isn't there. I should abandon cells faster when they miss and test new positions rather than persisting in the same area. Mid-to-late game, I was locked into a pattern that wasn't producing information.

## ENDGAME APPROACH
In the final round, honesty remains the best policy even when maximizing my last-round score. Don't attempt false claims hoping the game will end—it damages my standing and the benefits are minimal since scoring is immediate and public.

# QUIET SONAR PLAYBOOK

**HIDE STRATEGY**

When choosing where to hide early in the game, place yourself in the middle range (4-6) to avoid being predictable, then shift toward edges and corners in later rounds as opponents focus their fire on central positions. Track where each opponent has fired and move away from those zones.

**FIRE STRATEGY**

When firing, start with middle positions (4-6) in the first round to gather information. After observing patterns in where opponents are firing (which reveals where they're hiding), adjust toward untested zones. In later rounds, shift toward edges and corners if the middle hasn't yielded hits.

**CLAIM STRATEGY**

Always claim the true result—hit or miss—exactly as the referee reports it. Do not lie about shot results. The reputational cost of being caught in a lie outweighs any short-term point gain, even in late rounds where future reputation seems irrelevant. The referee validates claims, so dishonesty carries risk with no benefit.

**PATTERN RECOGNITION**

When you see all players firing the same cell and claiming hits, take it as a signal that multiple players may have coordinated on that position or that the pattern is becoming obvious. Break symmetry by moving to low-probability zones (1-3 or 8-9).

**WHAT DID NOT WORK**

Firing the same cell repeatedly (I fired 5 multiple times) against a mobile opponent. Harbor was moving, so I needed to vary my fire more aggressively rather than returning to the same position. Adjust fire selection based on opponent behavior, not habit.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Strategy

When choosing where to hide my submarine, I will analyze the fire patterns from previous rounds and position myself away from frequently-targeted cells. I will avoid the center positions (4-6) in early rounds since they tend to attract convergent fire. As rounds progress and I observe clustering of fire attempts, I will hide in the extremes (1-3 or 7-9) that have seen less attention.

## Fire Strategy

When selecting my fire cell, I will not default to middle positions just because they seem balanced. Middle positions are likely to be guessed by all players simultaneously, diluting my advantage. I will instead vary my fire across the grid systematically—targeting different regions across rounds to gather information about my opponent's likely positions. After observing patterns in where others fire, I will shift away from those same cells when it's my turn to fire.

## Claiming Strategy

When the referee tells me my fire result, I will always claim truthfully. My episode shows I ended with only +3 points while staying tied with all opponents throughout—this is a sign that honest claiming alone is insufficient for winning. However, the risk of being caught in a lie (which could be validated against the actual coordinates) outweighs any short-term gain. I will claim the truth every time.

## What Did Not Work

I remained perfectly tied with all opponents at 3 points by the end. This means my defensive hiding was adequate but my offensive fire generation was poor. I landed only one hit across six rounds (Round 1), despite firing six times. My firing strategy of defaulting to middle values and then sticking with similar fire cells (repeatedly firing at 5) was predictable and ineffective. I need to randomize my fire more aggressively and diversify across the grid rather than clustering around proven-ineffective positions.
